tagline: A curriculum is a delivery system for attention.

domains.name: The Deep Work Study Protocol
domains.summary: How the site teaches: the curriculum as an attention delivery system — distraction-free design, the one-module rhythm, attention training, artifact metrics, and slow-productivity pacing.

scenarios.title: The Device Rules
scenarios.situation: Leo opens a 90-minute study module with his phone on the desk (notifications on), twelve tabs open, and a group chat pinging. He reads the whole module and feels he 'studied.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the protocol say about his side of the bargain?
choices: He broke it. The site holds up its end by never manufacturing a distraction — no feed, no recommendations, no autoplay — and the protocol asks the learner to hold up theirs: notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open. The page cannot silence his phone; the device rules are his half of the design.
His setup is fine — willpower handles notifications.
The protocol only governs the site's design, not the learner.
He should study on his phone instead, since it's always with him.
scenarios.why: Distraction-free by design is a two-party contract. The curriculum is engineered as a delivery system for sustained attention — long-form pages, no engagement machinery, the page you opened is the page you study — but it assumes the device rules from the deep-work track. A site that never distracts you plus a phone that constantly does is still a distracted session.
scenarios.hint: Which half of the contract did Leo keep?

scenarios.title: One Module, One Session
scenarios.situation: Aisha has 45 minutes before work. She opens a module, skims half, switches to another track's module for variety, then answers email 'while she's at it.' She logs 'two modules touched.'
choices: Wrong rhythm on every axis: one module, one deep session. A module is a single long-form page because the material is cognitively demanding and needs unbroken time — she should have done one module fully (or none), with the session ending when the module ends. Half-modules and interleaved tracks are how dependency chains break.
Her approach is efficient — variety keeps the brain fresh.
She should have skimmed faster to finish both modules.
Email during study is fine if the replies are short.
scenarios.why: The study rhythm is one module, one deep session: the page's length is deliberate, the session's boundary is the module's end, and switching tracks mid-session is attention residue by design. 'Modules touched' is a vanity metric; the rhythm exists so each module's prerequisites are actually met before the next builds on them.
scenarios.hint: What will Aisha have built by the end of those 45 minutes?

scenarios.title: Hours vs. Artifacts
scenarios.situation: Two learners report their month. Ben logged 120 study hours (videos watched, pages scrolled). Cara logged 40 hours — and produced 12 lab artifacts, 4 re-derived proofs, and a working project.
scenarios.prompt: Who does the protocol judge as further along?
choices: Cara, unambiguously. Depth metrics: done means artifacts, not hours. Hours measure exposure; artifacts measure capability. Ben has 120 hours of familiarity; Cara has 40 hours of evidence — and only evidence compounds into the next module's prerequisites.
Ben — 120 hours is three times the effort.
Tie — both put in real work.
Ben, because consistency of hours predicts long-term success.
scenarios.why: The protocol's metric commitment is explicit: artifacts, not hours. A lab completed, a proof re-derived by hand, a fuzzer that found a real bug — these are the units of done. Hours are input; artifacts are output. Any system that rewards the input gets the input optimized and the output faked.
scenarios.hint: If both applied for the same role tomorrow, whose evidence would you hire on?

scenarios.title: The Sprint-and-Burn Semester
scenarios.situation: A study group plans their semester: ignore the material for ten weeks, then a two-week cram sprint before finals — energy drinks, all-nighters, twelve-hour days.
scenarios.prompt: What does slow-productivity pacing prescribe instead?
choices: The opposite arc: fewer obligations carried at once, work at a natural pace across the whole semester, obsessive focus on quality per module — one module per deep session, artifacts as gates. Sustainable depth beats sprint-and-burn because attention is trainable only under consistent load, and cramming produces familiarity that evaporates before the final that matters: actual capability.
The sprint plan is fine — pressure produces focus.
Extend the sprint to three weeks for safety.
Cramming works if you take good notes during the sprint.
scenarios.why: Slow productivity is the pacing layer of the protocol: do fewer things, at a natural pace, obsessing over quality. It is not slowness for its own sake — it is the recognition that depth compounds and cramming doesn't. A semester paced this way ends with artifacts; a sprint ends with exhaustion and evaporating familiarity.
scenarios.hint: What will the group remember — and be able to do — four weeks after the sprint?

scenarios.title: Auditing a Curriculum
scenarios.situation: You're asked to audit a commercial course platform against the five commitments: distraction-free by design, the study rhythm, attention training in the curriculum, depth metrics, and slow-productivity pacing. The platform has autoplay, infinite recommendations, streak counters, and 'completion' for watching videos.
choices: It fails all five, structurally. Autoplay and recommendations manufacture the fragmentation the protocol forbids; streak counters reward hours and clicks instead of artifacts; video-watch 'completion' inverts the depth metric; and the engagement machinery makes slow, deliberate pacing impossible. The platform is engineered against the learner — every mechanism that keeps users on the platform fragments the attention the material requires.
It passes — engagement features help learners stay motivated.
It passes four of five; only the metrics need tweaking.
The audit is inconclusive without A/B test data.
scenarios.why: The five commitments are a checklist you can hold any curriculum to — including this site. Distraction-free design means the missing features are missing deliberately; the rhythm means modules are session-sized; attention training means the curriculum teaches focus as a skill; depth metrics mean artifacts gate progress; pacing means the arc is sustainable. A platform optimized for engagement cannot satisfy them, because engagement and attention are competing objectives.
scenarios.hint: Which of the five could survive autoplay? Which couldn't?

scenarios.title: Your Own Protocol
scenarios.situation: After studying the protocol, you want to run your own study life on the same five commitments for the next 90 days — across job-hunt prep, a certification track, and an open-source project.
scenarios.prompt: What does a complete personal protocol specify?
choices: All five, operationalized: the environment contract (device rules, one tab, phone away — your half of the bargain); the rhythm (one module per deep session, session ends when the module ends); attention training (weekly deep-hour targets that ratchet up, boredom tolerance practice); the metric (artifact quotas per week, hours explicitly not counted); and the pacing (fixed shutdown, sustainable weekly load, quarterly review of artifacts produced). Plus the review loop that holds you to it.
A stricter app blocker and longer study hours.
Copying the site's track pages exactly as your schedule.
Studying whenever motivation strikes, but with the phone away.
scenarios.why: The protocol is stated publicly so learners can hold the site to it — and run their own study life on the same rules. A personal protocol needs each commitment as a mechanism, not an aspiration: environment rules, session boundaries, training targets, artifact quotas, pacing guardrails, and a review that checks the artifacts. Ninety days of that is a different education than ninety days of hours.
scenarios.hint: Which commitment would your current routine fail first?

domains.name: Lesson Sequences
domains.summary: The lesson layer under every learning path: how ordered lesson sequences structure learning across tracks — sequencing pedagogy, dependency chains, gates, capstones, and building your own sequences.

scenarios.title: Order the Modules
scenarios.situation: You're assembling a study sequence on container orchestration. The candidate modules are: 'Deploy your first pod,' 'Kubernetes architecture: control plane and nodes,' 'Services and networking,' 'What is a container?' A colleague suggests alphabetical order.
scenarios.prompt: What ordering does sequencing pedagogy demand?
choices: Dependency order: 'What is a container?' → 'Kubernetes architecture' → 'Deploy your first pod' → 'Services and networking.' Each module's prerequisites must be satisfied by earlier modules; alphabetical order strands the learner at module one.
Alphabetical — it's the only neutral ordering.
Hardest first, to filter out unserious learners.
Random order — self-paced learners can jump anywhere anyway.
scenarios.why: A lesson sequence is an ordered progression where each step's prerequisites are met by earlier steps. The sequence layer sits under every learning path on the site for exactly this reason: order is pedagogy. Alphabetical, chronological-by-publication, or difficulty-shuffled orderings all break the dependency chain the learner is climbing.
scenarios.hint: Which module can the learner not understand without the one before it?

scenarios.title: The Cramming Sequence
scenarios.situation: A learner plans to 'complete' a 12-module sequence on networking in one weekend: 12 modules, 12 hours of video-speed reading, no labs, no self-checks, straight through.
choices: Everything the sequence is for: one module per deep session is the rhythm — each module needs unbroken time, a lab, and self-checks before the next builds on it. Twelve modules in a weekend produces exposure, not the dependency chain the sequence promises. Slow, artifact-producing pacing is the design, not a suggestion.
Nothing — finishing fast shows motivation.
Only the labs break; the reading still counts as completion.
The weekend is too short; two weekends would fix it.
scenarios.why: Sequences are self-paced but not pace-free: the site's study rhythm is one module, one deep session, with labs and self-checks as the gates between steps. Cramming collapses the gates. Depth metrics decide completion — artifacts produced, not hours logged or modules clicked.
scenarios.hint: What will the learner have produced by Sunday night?

scenarios.title: Where Does the Capstone Go?
scenarios.situation: You're finalizing a sequence on applied cryptography. Modules cover: symmetric crypto, hashes, public-key, TLS, and a capstone project (audit a small system's crypto usage). A reviewer suggests putting the capstone second 'to motivate learners early.'
scenarios.prompt: Where does the capstone belong, and why?
choices: Last. A capstone synthesizes the whole dependency chain — it is the proof the sequence worked. Placing it early turns it into a teaser that the learner cannot yet do; the motivation it provides is frustration, not momentum. Early modules motivate through small, completable wins instead.
Second — early motivation outweighs pedagogy.
It doesn't matter; self-paced learners skip around anyway.
Split it across every module as micro-capstones with no final synthesis.
scenarios.why: Sequencing pedagogy distinguishes synthesis from motivation. Early modules earn momentum through completable labs and self-checks; the capstone earns its position at the end as the integrative artifact. A sequence that never synthesizes is a playlist, not a curriculum.
scenarios.hint: What can the learner only do after the *last* module that they couldn't do after the second?

scenarios.title: The Missing Prerequisite
scenarios.situation: Learners keep stalling at module 7 of your systems-programming sequence ('Write a minimal allocator'). Forum posts show they never actually learned pointer arithmetic — module 3 ('Memory and pointers') was marked 'optional background.'
choices: Promote the prerequisite into the chain: make module 3 required, add a self-check gate proving pointer fluency, and only then unlock the allocator module. A sequence is only as strong as its weakest assumed prerequisite — 'optional background' is where dependency chains go to die.
Make module 7 easier so the prerequisite doesn't matter.
Add a forum post explaining pointers and link it from module 7.
Remove module 7; allocators are too advanced.
scenarios.why: Every module implicitly asserts 'the learner can now do X.' When that assertion is false, everything downstream is theater. The fix is structural — required module, verifiable gate — not a link or a hint. Audit sequences by testing the assertion at each step, not by reading the titles.
scenarios.hint: Which assertion did module 7 make about the learner that wasn't true?

scenarios.title: Design a New Sequence
scenarios.situation: You've been asked to design a from-scratch 8-module sequence teaching 'Terraform and Infrastructure-as-Code' to working sysadmins. No existing sequence covers it on the site.
scenarios.prompt: What does a sound design process look like?
choices: Start from the terminal artifact: what the learner builds in the capstone (e.g. a versioned, reviewed, applied multi-environment setup). Work backward through the dependency chain — HCL syntax → state → modules → remote backends → plan/apply workflow → testing → policy → the capstone. Each module gets one deep session, a lab producing an artifact, and a self-check gate; then order strictly by dependency and cut anything that serves no downstream module.
List eight interesting Terraform topics and order them by personal preference.
Record eight lectures and call it a sequence.
Copy another site's course outline module for module.
scenarios.why: Backward design from the capstone artifact is the method: the end state defines the chain, the chain defines the modules, and each module earns its place by serving a downstream step. One module, one deep session, one artifact, one gate — then ruthless cutting of anything decorative. That is how a sequence becomes a curriculum instead of a content pile.
scenarios.hint: If a module disappeared, which later module would break?

scenarios.title: Remixing Existing Sequences
scenarios.situation: A learner wants 'the fastest path to productive Kubernetes work' and proposes stitching modules from three existing sequences: Linux System Administration, Docker and Container Engineering, and Kubernetes Certified Administrator — taking 'the interesting parts' of each.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build the remix responsibly?
choices: Extract the dependency chain, not the interesting parts: map every candidate module's prerequisites, keep the full chain for each kept module (pulling prerequisites from their home sequences), order by dependency, add one integrative capstone, and verify each gate still holds. A remix is a new sequence and must be re-validated as one — cherry-picking orphans modules from the prerequisites that made them learnable.
Take the interesting parts — motivation matters more than prerequisites.
Just do all three sequences end to end; remixes are never worth it.
Take only the capstones from each sequence.
scenarios.why: Sequences compose, but only through their dependency chains. The 'interesting parts' approach is how learners end up at module 7 without module 3. The responsible remix re-derives the chain across sequence boundaries, re-hangs the gates, and ends with its own synthesis — because the lesson layer under every path only works when the order is load-bearing.
scenarios.hint: For each 'interesting' module, where do its prerequisites live?

lessons.title: The Deep Work Study Protocol — Core concepts
concepts: A curriculum is a delivery system for attention. Most online learning is engineered against the learner — feeds, autoplay, streaks fragment the attention the material requires; this protocol inverts every one of those choices.

Distraction-free by design: long-form module pages, no feed, no recommendations, no autoplay, no notification layer. The missing features are missing deliberately — a learning platform should earn its place by serving deep work, and every feature that doesn't is a liability.

The contract has two parties: the site never manufactures a distraction; the learner brings the device rules — notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open. The page cannot silence your phone.
The study rhythm: one module, one deep session. The module's length is deliberate — cognitively demanding material needs unbroken time — and the session ends when the module ends.
Attention training is part of the curriculum: focus is treated as a trainable skill with targets that ratchet up, not as a fixed trait or a matter of willpower.
Depth metrics: done means artifacts, not hours. Labs completed, proofs re-derived, systems built — hours measure exposure, artifacts measure capability, and only capability compounds.
Slow-productivity pacing: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality. Sustainable depth across a semester beats sprint-and-burn; cramming produces familiarity that evaporates.

example.code:
mkdir -p ~/protocol && cat > ~/protocol/my-protocol.md <<'EOF'
# My 90-day study protocol
## 1. Environment contract
- Phone in another room, notifications off, one tab open.
## 2. Rhythm
- One module, one deep session. Session ends when the module ends.
## 3. Attention training
- Deep-hour target: 8/week, +1 every 2 weeks. Boredom practice: no phone in queues.
## 4. Depth metric (artifacts, NOT hours)
- Weekly artifact quota: 2. This week's: ___, ___
## 5. Pacing
- Fixed shutdown 21:30. Max 2 active tracks. Quarterly artifact review.
EOF
cat ~/protocol/my-protocol.md
example.walkthrough: Write the five commitments as mechanisms, not aspirations: environment rules, session boundaries, ratcheting attention targets, a weekly artifact quota with hours explicitly excluded, and pacing guardrails. The file is the protocol — review it weekly against the artifacts you actually produced.

pitfalls: Common trap: keeping the site's half of the contract while breaking yours. A distraction-free page plus a buzzing phone is still a distracted session.
Common trap: 'modules touched' as progress. Half-modules and interleaved tracks break the rhythm and the dependency chain.
Common trap: optimizing hours. Any system that rewards input gets input optimized and output faked — count artifacts.
Common trap: sprint-and-burn pacing dressed up as ambition. Depth compounds under consistent load; cramming evaporates.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: run a distraction-free session audit, then write your 90-day protocol with artifact quotas.

lessons.title: Lesson Sequences — Core concepts
concepts: A lesson sequence is the lesson layer under every learning path: an ordered progression of modules where each step's prerequisites are satisfied by earlier steps. Order is pedagogy, not packaging.

Dependency order is the only honest ordering. Alphabetical, by-publication, or difficulty-shuffled orders strand the learner; every module implicitly asserts what the learner can now do, and the chain must make that assertion true.
One module, one deep session: each module gets unbroken time, a lab producing an artifact, and a self-check gate before the next module builds on it. The gates are what make the chain trustworthy.
Capstones synthesize at the end. Early modules motivate through small completable wins; placing synthesis early produces frustration, not momentum. A sequence that never synthesizes is a playlist.
Prerequisites are structural, not advisory. 'Optional background' is where dependency chains die — promote the prerequisite, add a verifiable gate, then unlock the downstream module.

Design backward from the capstone artifact: the end state defines the chain, the chain defines the modules. Remix across sequences only by re-deriving the full dependency chain and re-validating every gate.

example.code:
mkdir -p ~/sequences && cat > ~/sequences/tf-sequence.md <<'EOF'
# Terraform & IaC — 8-module sequence (backward-designed)
# Capstone: versioned, reviewed, applied multi-env setup
1. HCL syntax & resource blocks        [lab: first config, artifact: main.tf]
2. State: what it is, why it bites       [lab: state surgery in sandbox]
3. plan/apply workflow                  [lab: plan review drill, gate: read a plan]
4. Variables, outputs, modules          [lab: refactor to module, artifact]
5. Remote backends & locking            [lab: team backend setup]
6. Workspaces vs directory-per-env      [lab: two-env layout, gate: justify choice]
7. Testing & policy (validate/test/sentinel) [lab: policy gate]
8. CAPSTONE: multi-env reviewed apply   [artifact: repo + runbook]
# Rule: module N's prerequisites all live in modules < N.
EOF
cat ~/sequences/tf-sequence.md
example.walkthrough: Sketch the sequence as a dependency-ordered list, each line carrying its lab artifact and any gate. The trailing rule is the whole discipline in one line: nothing in module N may assume knowledge that only appears later. Write it, then audit it by deleting each module and asking what breaks.

pitfalls: Common trap: ordering by topic popularity instead of dependency. Interesting-first strands learners at the first hard prerequisite.
Common trap: 'optional background' prerequisites. If a downstream module needs it, it is required — make it a module with a gate.
Common trap: capstone-as-teaser. Synthesis belongs at the end; early motivation comes from completable wins.
Common trap: counting clicked modules as completed. Done means artifacts produced and gates passed, not pages visited.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: map the dependency chain of a sequence you care about, then backward-design your own 6-module sequence.

labs.title: Session audit: run the contract for a week
labs.objective: Test the two-party distraction contract in real sessions for seven days and measure what changes.
steps: Create ~/protocol/session-audit.md with columns: date, module, deep minutes, contract kept? (device rules), artifacts produced.
For seven days, run study sessions under the full contract: notifications off, phone in another room, one tab open, one module per session.
Log every session honestly — including the ones where you broke the contract and why.
Total your deep minutes and artifacts; compare against a normal week from memory.
Write a verdict paragraph: which half of the contract (yours) failed most, and the one fix you'll keep.

checks.hint: cat your session-audit.md and confirm artifacts (not hours) are logged per session.
Confirm seven days of entries exist (grep -c).

labs.title: Artifact audit: depth metrics on your last month
labs.objective: Apply depth metrics retroactively: inventory last month's artifacts vs. hours and set next month's artifact quota.
steps: List everything you produced last month that counts as an artifact: labs, proofs, projects, working systems, published notes.
Estimate the hours spent; compute nothing fancy — just place the two lists side by side in ~/protocol/artifact-audit.md.
Grade the month by the protocol's metric: what compounded (usable in the next module) vs. what evaporated?
Set next month's artifact quota: a specific number of specific artifact types — hours explicitly excluded from the target.
Print the audit and read the quota aloud; it should name artifacts, not hours.

checks.hint: cat artifact-audit.md and confirm the artifact quota names artifact types, not hours.
Confirm the artifact inventory lists concrete produced work.

labs.title: Sequence audit: map a dependency chain
labs.objective: Take an existing multi-module sequence and verify every module's prerequisites are satisfied by earlier modules.
steps: Pick a sequence you are studying (on this site or elsewhere) with at least 6 modules.
Create ~/sequences/audit.md listing each module and the concrete skills it assumes.
For each assumed skill, trace it to the earlier module that teaches it — mark any assumption with no source module as ORPHANED.
For every orphaned assumption, write the fix: promote it to a module, add a gate, or re-order.
Print the audit and count: modules, traced prerequisites, orphaned assumptions, proposed fixes.

checks.hint: cat your audit and confirm orphaned assumptions are marked (or explicitly zero).
Verify the file lists modules and traced prerequisites (grep -c).

labs.title: Build your own 6-module sequence
labs.objective: Backward-design a 6-module sequence on a topic you want to learn, with capstone, artifacts, and gates.
steps: Define the capstone artifact: what you will have built or be able to do at the end.
Work backward: list the dependency chain the capstone requires, in strict prerequisite order.
Compress or expand the chain to exactly 6 modules; each gets one lab artifact and one self-check gate.
Write the sequence to ~/sequences/my-sequence.md with the dependency rule stated at the bottom.
Delete-test: for each module, confirm which later module breaks without it; cut any module whose deletion breaks nothing.

checks.hint: cat my-sequence.md and confirm the capstone artifact is defined.
Confirm each module names its artifact and gate (grep for 'artifact').

behavioral.prompt: How do you structure your own learning when you need to master something hard?
behavioral.framework: The protocol, personalized: environment, rhythm, attention training, artifact metrics, pacing — with evidence it works.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you eliminated distractions to do deep work. What changed?
behavioral.framework: STAR: the fragmented baseline, the contract (both halves), the measured change in output quality.

behavioral.prompt: How do you know when you've actually learned something versus just being familiar with it?
behavioral.framework: Artifacts not hours: what you produced, what you can now do unaided, the test you set yourself.
pitfalls: Hours or pages as the metric
'I understood it when I read it'

behavioral.prompt: Describe your ideal work environment for cognitively demanding tasks.
behavioral.framework: Environment design: device rules, session boundaries, interruption protocols, what you ask of others.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a period where you sustained focused effort over months. How did you pace it?
behavioral.framework: Slow-productivity framing: sustainable load, fixed boundaries, quality obsession, the compounding result.

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle the tension between urgent messages and important deep work?
behavioral.framework: Batched communication, defined urgency paths, expectations set — protecting depth without going dark.

behavioral.prompt: Describe something you built or produced that you're proud of. What did 'done' mean?
behavioral.framework: The artifact, the quality bar, the review it survived — done as evidence, not effort.

behavioral.prompt: If you were designing onboarding for a new team member, how would you structure their first 90 days?
behavioral.framework: Protocol thinking applied to others: environment, rhythm, artifact milestones, paced load, review cadence.

cheatsheet: Curriculum = attention delivery system. Engagement and attention are competing objectives.
Distraction-free by design: the missing features are missing deliberately.
Two-party contract: the site never distracts; you bring the device rules.
One module, one deep session. Session ends when the module ends.
Attention is trainable: targets ratchet up, boredom tolerance is practice.
Done = artifacts, not hours. Hours are input; artifacts compound.
Slow productivity: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality.

glossary.def: The five commitments shaping every track, module, and lab: distraction-free design, rhythm, attention training, depth metrics, pacing.
A measure of capability produced (artifacts), as opposed to input consumed (hours).
A produced unit of evidence: a completed lab, a re-derived proof, a working system, published notes.
One module per deep session; the session boundary is the module's end.
The learner's half of the contract: notifications off, phone away, one tab open.

checklist: I can state all five commitments from memory.
My study environment satisfies the device rules.
I run one module per deep session and stop at the module's end.
My progress metric counts artifacts, not hours.
My semester/quarter is paced for sustainable depth.

chat.persona: A study-protocol coach: warm but exacting, counts your artifacts instead of your hours, always asking which half of the contract you kept today.

simulations.title: Why Did the Study Week Fail?
simulations.brief: You 'studied' 25 hours this week and failed the practice exam. Diagnose the protocol failure.

steps.symptom: 25 logged hours, practice exam score 52% (passing is 70%).
evidence: 18 hours re-reading notes, 5 hours highlighting, 2 hours practice questions
Can define terms, cannot apply them to new problems
No spaced intervals — everything crammed in 3 days
options: Not enough hours — push to 35 next week
Fluency illusion: re-reading and highlighting build recognition, not recall — the protocol optimized for the feeling of learning, and massed cramming guaranteed forgetting
steps.explain: Re-reading produces fluency (it feels known) without retrievability. The evidence: definitions without application. The protocol must swap recognition activities for retrieval activities and distribute them over time.

steps.symptom: You switch to practice questions. Scores rise to 64% but plateau. What's the missing mechanism?
evidence: Wrong answers re-read once, never re-tested
options: Error-driven spaced repetition: each misconception becomes a flashcard scheduled at expanding intervals until it's answered correctly three times cold
steps.explain: Plateaus come from uncorrected misconceptions. The fix is a system: errors → cards → spaced schedule → cold-correct ×3. Volume without an error loop just rehearses the same mistakes faster.

steps.symptom: New protocol designed. What single weekly metric proves it's working before the next exam?
evidence: Predicts exam performance, not just effort
options: Cold recall rate: percentage of due flashcards answered correctly with no hints, tracked weekly
steps.explain: Cold recall rate measures the actual asset (retrievable knowledge), not the input (hours) or the exhaust (notes). If it climbs 5% a week, the exam takes care of itself.

simulations.debrief: Study protocols fail on fluency (recognition ≠ recall), massing (cramming ≠ learning), and missing error loops. The fix: retrieval practice, spaced intervals, error cards, and one honest metric.

simulations.title: Choose the Method
simulations.brief: A brutal certification exam in 8 weeks. Four study methods compete for your 15 hours/week. Allocate like an engineer.

steps.text: 15 hrs/week, 8 weeks. Options: (A) video course end-to-end, (B) textbook cover-to-cover, (C) practice-exam-driven with targeted remediation, (D) study group discussions. Your allocation?

choices.label: A — videos feel productive and cover everything
choices.feedback: Videos are the re-reading of the digital age: high fluency, low retrieval. Eight weeks later you'll recognize everything and recall nothing under pressure.

choices.label: C — practice exams first, then remediate exactly what fails
choices.feedback: The exam is the specification: test early, let failures aim your studying, remediate with focused retrieval. Every hour targets a measured gap.

choices.label: B — the textbook is the complete source of truth
choices.feedback: Complete and unfinishable: 900 pages in 8 weeks at 15 hrs/week means skimming, and skimming means fluency without recall.

steps.text: Week 5: you've 'covered' 70% of the material but your first practice exam scores 58%. Panic is setting in. Repair?

choices.label: Speed up — finish the remaining 30% then do practice exams
choices.feedback: More coverage of the same passive method. The 58% isn't a coverage problem; it's a retrieval problem.

choices.label: Stop covering; switch to exam-driven remediation now — 3 weeks of targeted retrieval beats 3 weeks of finishing videos
choices.feedback: The correct late-stage pivot: abandon coverage, attack measured gaps. Triage beats completion.

steps.text: Week 5: practice scores 76% and climbing. But networking questions sit at 40% while everything else is 80%+. Your move?

choices.label: Keep the balanced rotation — it'll come up naturally
choices.feedback: The data names the gap; ignoring it is choosing to fail networking. Balanced feels fair; targeted wins.

choices.label: Reallocate: 60% of hours to networking until it hits 70%, maintenance reps for the rest
choices.feedback: Data-driven reallocation: attack the weakest link, maintain the rest with spaced reps. This is what the protocol is FOR.

simulations.debrief: Study like an engineer: the exam is the spec, practice tests are the test suite, failures are the bug reports, and your hours are the sprint capacity. Allocate to the red tests.

simulations.title: Build the Study Session
simulations.brief: Order the five moves of a 90-minute protocol study session.

steps.context: One 90-minute session, one topic. Order the moves for maximum durable learning.
items: Warm up with 10 minutes of cold recall on yesterday's material (no notes)
Attempt new problems BEFORE consulting references — struggle first
Check answers and convert every error into a spaced-repetition card
Do a 5-minute free-recall brain dump of the session's key ideas
Log the session: what was learned, what's still shaky, tomorrow's target

simulations.debrief: Recall before reference (warm-up), struggle before help (desirable difficulty), errors into cards (the loop), brain dump (consolidation), log (tomorrow's start). The session is a pipeline, not a vibe.

simulations.title: Audit the Study Plan
simulations.brief: A study plan for a certification exam has 3 protocol violations. Find them.

steps.config:
# study-plan.conf — 8 week cert prep
method = reread_notes            # line 2
schedule = cram_weekends          # line 3
retrieval = none                  # line 4
error_cards = 0                   # line 5
practice_exams = 1                # line 6
sleep = 5h                        # line 7
review = weekly                   # line 8

issues.description: Method is re-reading notes — pure fluency, zero retrieval. The plan optimizes for feeling prepared.
issues.fix: method = retrieval_practice (cold recall, practice questions, brain dumps).

issues.description: Crammed weekends — massed practice guarantees maximum forgetting between sessions.
issues.fix: schedule = distributed daily blocks with spaced intervals.

issues.description: No retrieval practice at all — the single highest-evidence study technique is entirely absent.
issues.fix: retrieval = every session starts with cold recall.

simulations.debrief: Lines 5–8 are also weak (no error cards, one practice exam, 5h sleep) but the three flagged lines are the structural violations: no retrieval, massed schedule, fluency-based method. Fix the method first.

simulations.title: Exam Week Triage
simulations.brief: The exam is in 72 hours. Your cold-recall rate is 68%; passing needs ~75%. Triage the final three days.

steps.text: 72 hours left. Cold recall 68%, need 75%. Your error cards cluster in two domains: subnetting (55%) and IAM policies (61%). Everything else is 75%+. The plan?

choices.label: Re-read all the notes once more for confidence
choices.feedback: Confidence without recall is how you walk in at 68% and walk out at 68%. The data is begging you to target.

choices.label: All retrieval, all gaps: drill subnetting and IAM cards at tight intervals, one full practice exam at hour 48, sleep 8h nightly
choices.feedback: The triage protocol: attack the measured gaps, verify with a full exam, protect sleep — the highest-ROI 72 hours available.

choices.label: Pull two all-nighters — more hours is more learning
choices.feedback: Sleep deprivation destroys exactly what the exam tests: recall under pressure. You'd trade 5 points of knowledge for 10 points of impairment.

steps.text: 24 hours left and you're exhausted, scoring 66% on drills — worse than three days ago. Emergency move?

choices.label: Caffeine and one more all-nighter — push through
choices.feedback: Pushing through impairment is how 68% becomes 60%. The exam punishes exactly this.

choices.label: Stop. Sleep 8 hours, light review only, trust the base — damage control beats more damage
choices.feedback: The least-bad move: sleep restores recall more than any cramming recovers. You sit the exam at your true 68% instead of an impaired 60%.

steps.text: Hour 48 practice exam: 77%. The gaps closed. Last 24 hours — what now?

choices.label: Learn a brand-new topic to 'maximize coverage'
choices.feedback: New topics at hour 48 create interference and anxiety. The exam rewards depth on the spec, not breadth beyond it.

choices.label: Light maintenance reps, review error cards once, pack your bag, sleep early — arrive at 100% of your 77%
choices.feedback: The professional finish: protect the gains, arrive rested. Exams are won in the 8 weeks before, and lost in the 24 hours before.

simulations.debrief: Exam-week triage: drill the measured gaps, verify with a full practice exam, protect sleep absolutely. The protocol's final lesson — performance is retrieval plus rest, and rest is not negotiable.

consoleSims.title: Organize the Study Archive
consoleSims.brief: Your study materials need archival order: a subjects directory, a protected error-log file, and locked permissions.

tasks.instruction: Create the file /home/user/study/error-log.txt — every misconception gets logged here.
Set mode 600 on /home/user/study/error-log.txt — your error log is private.
tasks.hint: Select the file, then chmod with mode 600.

consoleSims.debrief: The protocol needs infrastructure: a study directory, an error log with a name that reminds you what it's for, and permissions that keep it yours.

consoleSims.title: Run the Study Pipeline
consoleSims.brief: Treat your study week like a pipeline: trigger the week's run, retry the failed recall stage, configure the target, ship the review.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build — this week's study run.
The 'test' stage (Friday's cold-recall check) failed — retry it.
Approve the gated 'deploy' stage — publish the week's review notes.

consoleSims.debrief: The study week as CI: trigger (start), retry (re-drill failures), variables (declare targets), approve (publish the review). Green builds compound.

consoleSims.title: Triage the Blocker Queue
consoleSims.brief: Study blockers are incidents. Log them, assign them, move them — don't ruminate on them.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Subnetting cold recall stuck at 55%'.
tasks.hint: New ticket: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P2.

consoleSims.debrief: Externalize the blockers: a ticketed gap gets a plan; a ruminated gap gets anxiety. The queue is where stuck becomes scheduled.

consoleSims.title: Review the Notes Repo
consoleSims.brief: Your study notes live under version control. Branch the week's review, open the PR, and merge the corrections.

tasks.instruction: Open a PR titled 'Week 5: fix 6 misconception notes' from head 'review/week-5-corrections' to base 'main'.
tasks.hint: Open PR: exact title, BASE main, HEAD review/week-5-corrections.

tasks.instruction: Merge PR #1 (the pre-seeded one) — clear the queue before your review lands.
tasks.hint: In Pull requests, click Merge on PR #1.

consoleSims.debrief: Notes under version control: corrections are PRs, misconceptions get fixed with history, and the log shows exactly when each idea became correct.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Desk
terminalMissions.brief: Orient: list the workspace and read the notes.
terminalMissions.success_message: Desk surveyed. The protocol starts with knowing the material.

terminalMissions.title: Start the Recall Log
terminalMissions.brief: Log cold-recall sessions to recall.txt — the protocol's honest instrument.

checks.hint: Type: echo "session1 recall 62pct" > recall.txt (no output on success).

terminalMissions.success_message: Recall log started. What gets measured gets learned.

terminalMissions.title: Measure the Trend
terminalMissions.brief: Count sessions and search the log — is recall climbing?
terminalMissions.success_message: Trend measured. Climbing cold-recall is the only progress that counts.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Target
terminalMissions.brief: Hash your exam-date target — commitment, tamper-evident.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum recall-75 by exam day — the real hash plus your target are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Target sealed. The protocol commits before the pressure arrives.

terminalMissions.title: Check the Session Edges
terminalMissions.brief: Review any log from its edges: first lines, last lines.
terminalMissions.success_message: Edges checked. Every review starts at the boundaries.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the Environment
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm the study environment: identity and home.

terminalMissions.title: Reach the Library
terminalMissions.brief: Verify the digital library resolves and responds.
terminalMissions.success_message: Library reachable. The protocol's supply line is open.
